title: Bit Manipulation
description: Using bitwise operators to set, clear, toggle, and check individual bits, and the role of bit masks.
objectives: Use bitwise operators to manipulate individual bits
Set, clear, toggle, and check specific bits

content.heading: Bitwise Operators and Masks
content.body:
The bitwise operators — & (AND), | (OR), ^ (XOR), ~ (NOT), << (left shift), >> (right shift) — operate on the individual binary bits of an integer's representation, independent of its value's usual arithmetic meaning. A bit mask is simply an integer value chosen specifically so that its bit pattern, combined with a target value via a bitwise operator, isolates, sets, or clears specific bit positions — e.g., 1 << 3 produces the mask 00001000 (binary), representing 'bit position 3'.

Bit manipulation is used for tightly packing multiple boolean flags into a single integer (common in embedded/systems programming where memory is constrained, or for representing hardware register flags), and for certain performance-sensitive algorithms where operating directly on bits avoids more expensive arithmetic or branching.

content.heading: Setting, Clearing, Toggling, and Checking Bits
content.body: Setting bit n (making it 1, regardless of its current value): value |= (1 << n) — OR-ing with a mask that has only that bit set forces it on, leaving other bits unchanged (since OR-ing anything with 0 leaves it unchanged). Clearing bit n (making it 0): value &= ~(1 << n) — AND-ing with the complement of the mask (all bits 1 except position n) forces that one bit off while leaving the rest unchanged (since AND-ing anything with 1 leaves it unchanged). Toggling bit n (flipping it): value ^= (1 << n) — XOR-ing with the mask flips exactly that bit (since XOR-ing with 0 leaves a bit unchanged, and XOR-ing with 1 flips it). Checking whether bit n is set: (value & (1 << n)) != 0 — AND-ing with the mask isolates that bit, leaving it as the only possibly-nonzero bit in the result.

content.explanation: Each operation demonstrates the standard idiom for its purpose: |= to set, &= ~ to clear, & to check, ^= to toggle — all built from the fundamental bitwise operators and a shifted mask.

keyPoints: Bitwise operators (&, |, ^, ~, <<, >>) manipulate an integer's individual binary bits directly
A bit mask, typically built with 1 << n, isolates a specific bit position for these operations
|= sets a bit, &= ~mask clears it, ^= toggles it, and & (!= 0) checks it
Bit manipulation is commonly used to pack multiple boolean flags compactly into one integer
commonMistakes: Confusing bitwise & / | with logical && / || (they behave very differently, especially on non-0/1 values)
Forgetting the ~ when clearing a bit, accidentally setting everything except the target bit instead
Off-by-one errors in the bit position used in a mask (1 << n for bit n, not 1 << (n-1) or similar)
